items.body: Swedish dark synthpop trio Priest will release the single “Python” on August 21 via Blue Nine, the first taste of their fifth studio album, “Altered State Police,” due October 23 on the same label. The announcement follows the band’s US tour supporting Stabbing Westward. “Python” turns surveillance and data collection into subject matter, built around relentless electronics, industrial textures and flashes of ’90s big beat. The track includes a spoken sequence cataloguing a listener’s data: “Terms accepted. Surveillance initiated. Facial data: stored. Iris response: logged. Voice patterns: catalogued. You are now a consumer profile. Thank you for agreeing.” Priest describe it as one of their most direct and danceable songs to date, addressing “what happens when we’ve accepted being watched without even noticing.” “Altered State Police” is designed as a continuous listening experience rather than a loose collection of songs, built around surveillance, political distrust, technological dependence and the boundary between human and machine, with songs written to answer questions raised elsewhere on the record. Neither the single nor the album has surfaced yet on Bandcamp, YouTube or Spotify; Priest’s official site, priestnexus.com, currently carries the “Python” and “Altered State Police” announcement and upcoming tour information. The single follows Priest’s run on the Wither ReWired Tour, the 2026 US trek on which Stabbing Westward re-recorded “Wither Blister Burn + Peel” for its 30th anniversary, with Priest and Acumen Nation as support. Priest ‘Python’: release details “Python” arrives August 21 via Blue Nine as the first single from “Altered State Police,” out October 23 on the same label. No tracklist, credits or formats for the album have been confirmed at the time of writing. About Priest Priest is a dark synthpop trio from Stockholm, Sweden, formed in 2017 by former members of Ghost: vocalist Mercury (previously the bassist known as Water in Ghost) and keyboardist Salt (previously the keyboardist known as Air in Ghost), later joined by keyboardist and programmer Sulfur. The band’s sound draws on 1980s sci-fi synth textures, gothic soundscapes and industrial and cyberpunk elements, distinct from Ghost’s horror-rock theatrics. Priest released its debut album, “New Flesh,” in 2017, followed by the “Obey” EP in 2019 and the album “Cyberhead” in 2020. The band signed to Cleopatra Records in 2021 and released the single “A Signal in the Noise” that December. Further releases include the “Chaos EP,” the live album “Live in Hollywood,” the studio album “Dark Pulse” and, in March 2026, “Body Machine.” Priest has since moved to the label Blue Nine, which issues “Python” and the forthcoming “Altered State Police.” Priest has toured internationally in support of its releases, most recently opening for Stabbing Westward’s Wither ReWired Tour across the United States in 2026. “Python,” out August 21, and “Altered State Police,” out October 23, mark the band’s next chapter under Blue Nine.

The band describes its own sound as “dark alternative.” The nine-track record went up on 14 July 2026, led by the single “We Should.” Luminance by My Black Heart Machine “Luminance” comprises nine tracks: “Bittersweet,” “Your Last Breath,” “Everytime,” “We Should,” “The Last Thing I’ll See,” “All Hail You,” “Your Shattered Mind,” “Luminance,” and “A Warm Light.” The album is available as a digital release through Bandcamp. My Black Heart Machine pairs ‘Luminance’ with a ‘We Should’ video The album’s first single, “We Should,” comes with an official music video posted to My Black Heart Machine’s own YouTube channel. About My Black Heart Machine My Black Heart Machine is the project of Camilo Montenegro, a composer, producer, and mixing engineer based in Mexico City, Mexico. Montenegro writes, arranges, and performs the material under the My Black Heart Machine name. The project’s prior album, “Anonymous Confessions,” came out on 2 January 2024 and ran ten tracks. “Luminance” is My Black Heart Machine’s newest full-length, released independently through Bandcamp.

items.body: Project Pitchfork, the German dark electro group fronted by Peter Spilles, gets a Project Pitchfork anthology vinyl release: two of its career-spanning compilations pressed to vinyl for the first time. Trisol releases “First Anthology” and “Second Anthology” as limited 3LP sets on 16 October 2026, each capped at 1,000 numbered copies. “First Anthology” was originally issued as a double CD in 2011, drawing on the band’s early years, its own label Candyland Entertainment and its later run on the major-label imprint EastWest. The new vinyl edition spreads 31 tracks across three 180g 12″ black vinyl records, a German audiophile pressing, and includes anthem tracks such as “Timekiller”, “Alpha Omega” and “I Live Your Dream”. The set comes in a gatefold sleeve with printed inner sleeves, and the artwork draws on photos from Peter Spilles’ private archive. “Second Anthology” followed in 2016 as a companion double CD covering the band’s catalogue from 2002 onward, built around the previously unreleased song “What Have We Done” and a remix, “Beholder (Puppet Master Mix)”. Its vinyl counterpart carries 30 tracks over three 180g 12″ records with the same gatefold, printed-inner-sleeve and archive-photo artwork treatment as its companion, and highlights key tracks “Rain”, “Acid Ocean” and “Beholder”. Both anthologies are limited to 1,000 numbered copies and are due through Trisol. Project Pitchfork anthology vinyl arrives ahead of anniversary tour The two anthology vinyls land in the same year Project Pitchfork mark their 35th anniversary. Side-Line previously reported on the band’s Dhyani 35th anniversary reissue, the 2LP deluxe edition of Entities, and the 35 Years in the Heart of Darkness anniversary tour running across Germany from October to December 2026 – the same window in which both anthology vinyls arrive. About Project Pitchfork Project Pitchfork was formed in Hamburg, Germany, by Peter Spilles and Dirk Scheuber, who met in late 1988 and began working together as Project Pitchfork the following year, picking the band’s name at random from a dictionary. The band played its first live show in Hamburg in February 1990 and released the demo “K.N.K.A.” that August. Debut album “Dhyani” followed in May 1991 on Hypnobeat, with second album “Lam-‘Bras” arriving in February 1992 and introducing Patricia Nigiani as a backing vocalist. Third album “Entities” followed six months later. A move to the Off Beat label produced 1994’s “Io,” which gave the band its first German chart entry via the singles “Renascence” and “Carrion,” followed by a lengthy tour. In 1995 Project Pitchfork founded their own label, Candyland Entertainment, releasing “Alpha Omega” the same year and touring in support of Rammstein. “¡Chakra:Red!” (1997) was the first album written as a full group effort and introduced Jürgen Jansen as a permanent member. The band then signed to major-label imprint EastWest for the concept album “Eon:Eon” (1998), whose singles “Steelrose,” “Carnival” and “I Live Your Dream” brought the band German music-TV airplay and an Echo Award nomination for the “Steelrose” video. Project Pitchfork released “Daimonion” (2001) and the “NUN” trilogy centered on “Inferno” (2002), then “Kaskade” (2005) and “Dream, Tiresias!” (2009). By 2011, having wound down Candyland, the band had moved to Trisol, releasing “Continuum Ride” (2010) and “Quantum Mechanics” (2011) – the same year Trisol issued the original “First Anthology” compilation. “Black” (2013) and “Blood” (2014) followed, and in 2016 Trisol released “Second Anthology,” built around the unreleased track “What Have We Done,” alongside 25th-anniversary album “Look Up, I’m Down There.” “Akkretion” (2018) and “Fragment” (2018) opened a further trilogy that closed with 2024’s “Elysium.” Co-founder Dirk Scheuber left the band in March 2021; the current lineup centers on Peter Spilles with Jürgen Jansen, alongside live drummers Achim Färber and Christian “Leo” Leonhardt. Trisol now brings both career-spanning anthologies to vinyl for the first time, due 16 October 2026 as limited, numbered 3LP editions.

items.body: Immersion, the electronic duo of Wire‘s Colin Newman and Minimal Compact‘s Malka Spigel, will release the album “What Is Lost Will Return” on September 4 via their own label, swim~. The record follows 2025’s “WTF??” and is the duo’s second “pure” Immersion release in as many years. The first single, “We Don’t Need Your Validation,” is out now with an official video. Newman and Spigel have described the track as being about “seeking validation in all the wrong places.” The album’s eight tracks are “Nephology,” “Breaking Free, Diversity, Evolution,” “We Don’t Need Your Validation,” “Megafauna,” “What Is Lost Will Return,” “Childsplay,” “Radio Signals” and “Frequencies & Echoes.” Core duo Newman and Spigel are joined on the record by drummer Matt Schulz (Holy Fuck), featured across several tracks, with Ed Chivers (AK/DK) guesting on drums on “Breaking Free, Diversity, Evolution.” Where “WTF??” leaned into disorientation, “What Is Lost Will Return” searches for what endures. Newman and Spigel describe the record as invoking “a poignant mixture of joy and melancholy.” “What Is Lost Will Return” is confirmed on vinyl LP and CD through swim~, alongside digital formats; the vinyl edition is pressed across two sides, with “Nephology” through “Megafauna” on side A and “What Is Lost Will Return” through “Frequencies & Echoes” on side B. The album arrives ahead of Immersion’s third UK tour since 2024. About Immersion Immersion is the long-running duo of Colin Newman, singer and guitarist of English post-punk band Wire, and Malka Spigel, formerly of Israeli post-punk group Minimal Compact; the two are also creative and life partners and run swim~ together. Immersion began in 1994, releasing albums on swim~ and staging video-driven live performances at venues including London’s Royal Festival Hall and New York’s Knitting Factory, before the project went dormant between 1999 and 2016. Since its 2016 return, Immersion has expanded into an ongoing series of collaborative “Nanocluster” albums and events, working with artists including Tarwater, Laetitia Sadier, Ulrich Schnauss, Scanner, Thor Harris, Cubzoa and SUSS; the latest instalment, “Nanocluster Vol. 3,” featured SUSS and was released in January 2025. Newman and Spigel also record together as Githead. In July 2025, Immersion announced the album “WTF??”, their first “pure,” non-collaborative release in that run. “What Is Lost Will Return,” out September 4, 2026 via swim~, is its follow-up and marks the duo’s third UK tour since 2024.

items.body: An ideal is usually sold as an aspiration: polished, desirable, harmless. Repeat it often enough, and it becomes a measurement of success; attach it to a nation, and it begins to sound like political doctrine. Who is seen, who is erased, and who gets classified as beautiful, useful, obedient, or disposable? PIG takes that glossy marketing phrase and feeds it through distortion, machine vision, and command. Out July 31st via Metropolis Records, “An American Ideal of Beauty” is the latest single from UK industrial glam maverick Raymond Watts, aka PIG. Co-written with old friend Marc Heal of Cubanate and C-Tec, who contributes co-vocals and synthesizers, the track also features Günter Schulz (ex-KMFDM) sharing guitar duties with Watts and his regular songwriting partner Jim Davies (ex-The Prodigy and Pitchshifter). “An American Ideal of Beauty” delivers classic industrial rock at full weight. Thick guitars grind against a regimented beat as synths jab through the arrangement and metal vocal growls force the lower register into something almost animal. Watts rises above the mass with his familiar theatrical vocal swagger, stretching syllables into decadent declarations before snapping back into clipped commands. Heal’s co-vocal adds another rough-edged authority, while Schulz and Davies keep the guitars dense, physical, and sharply defined. Watts explains: “I wanted to distill and hone the sound of the current PIG album, ‘Hurt People Hurt’, so inviting my old partners in swine Marc and Günter to join Jim and myself in the studio seemed the perfect blend of brutality and beauty to feed, fertilise and transmogrify the hog into Hogzilla. This new single was the first result of our work as a quartet, hammered in the heat of the anvil of hurt.” Directed by E Gabriel Edvy for Blackswitch Labs, the accompanying video makes looking itself feel coercive. Eyes and faces are boxed, duplicated, enlarged, and tagged with computer-vision graphics, as though every human feature were being measured by an automated judge. Watts performs within a narrow brick passage and against near-total blackness, his figure ruptured by washes of red, white, and electric blue. Words such as CHAOS, LIES, SHOOT, DUTY, BEAUTY, JESUS, INSURRECTION, and SHUT UP strike the screen as orders, accusations, and advertising copy. Human faces in harsh negative share space with horses, insects, forest growth, fire, floodwater, television static, isolated roads, and a sterile server corridor. The rapid editing expands the title beyond cosmetic standards, placing glamour, violence, faith, technology, and civic obedience inside the same system of classification. Beauty becomes another category assigned by the machine, with the viewer positioned as both observer and object of observation. Watch the video for An American Ideal of Beauty below: The recording sessions produced three additional songs, all of which join “An American Ideal of Beauty” on the forthcoming eight-track EP, Dirt Box. Its four originals are paired with remixes by Cyanotic, Stabbing Westward’s Chris Hall, Combichrist, and Rabbit Junk. Dirt Box arrives September 4th, 2026, through Metropolis Records and is available to pre-order through Bandcamp. “An American Ideal of Beauty” can be streamed here. The EP follows PIG’s current album, Hurt People Hurt, released May 22nd through Metropolis. Largely written by Watts and Davies, the record further develops PIG’s union of industrial force, dance-floor discipline, theatrical excess, and Watts’ barbed gallows humour. Watts has spent more than four decades working throughout industrial and alternative music. Alongside his extensive catalogue as PIG, he was a founding member of KMFDM and played a central writing and vocal role in the band’s work during the ’80s and ’90s. His collaborations have included Einstürzende Neubauten, Foetus, Psychic TV, Schwein, and Schaft, while his music for fashion has accompanied Alexander McQueen’s Plato’s Atlantis and the exhibitions Punk: Chaos to Couture and Savage Beauty. PIG will take Hurt People Hurt across North America beginning August 26th, with Cyanotic joining the tour. The itinerary includes appearances at Cold Waves XIV in Los Angeles, Austin, and Chicago, followed by four UK shows in December. items.album: London Trio Black Doldrums Share Video for Dirgeful Single “Repetition”
items.excerpt: “The doldrums” sounds like a dark room with no windows and no lights. You step inside, lock the door behind you, and extinguish the final seam of light beneath it. At first, the darkness appears empty; then the mind begins furnishing it with everything you hoped to leave outside. items.body: “The doldrums” sounds like a dark room with no windows and no lights. You step inside, lock the door behind you, and extinguish the final seam of light beneath it. At first, the darkness appears empty; then the mind begins furnishing it with everything you hoped to leave outside. Fear searches for something concealed nearby while dread waits for it to reveal itself. Angst returns to the same unanswered question, passion strains against confinement, love becomes fixation, and anguish grows louder because there is nowhere for any of it to go. Beyond that imagined room, the word describes a spell of listlessness or despondency, a period of stagnation, and an equatorial region of calms, squalls, and shifting winds. In its nautical sense, opposing trade winds converge near the equator, leaving sailing ships trapped on windless water. The sails collapse, the hull ceases to advance, provisions diminish, and the crew can see the horizon without drawing any closer to it. The ship and the dark room share one cruelty: an exit can be imagined while remaining unreachable. Goth and post-punk have made lasting music from precisely these states. Fear tightens the bass into a narrow repeating figure; dread occupies the interval before the next drum hit; angst gives the lyric a question it cannot answer; passion swells through distortion; love supplies the reason to remain; anguish comes from recognizing the pattern while continuing to obey it. Black Doldrums is therefore an unusually exact name: music for the locked room and a ship adrift at sea, where the mind returns to familiar pain because familiarity can resemble shelter. Appropriately, London trio Black Doldrums’ latest release, Repetition, centers on the inability to break a pattern. The song is the lead single and opening track of the band’s third studio album, Repetition Compulsion, due November 13th, 2026, via Fuzz Club. The record completes Black Doldrums’ interconnected “State of Mind Trilogy,” following their 2022 debut, Dead Awake, and 2024’s In Limerence. The three albums consider the psychological forces that shape identity, memory, and human connection, with the creative and personal partnership between founding members Kevin Gibbard and Sophie Landers providing their emotional center. As Gibbard explains: “The songs are either about Sophie, for Sophie, or inspired by her.” “Repetition begins with a funereal synthesizer exhalation, a dusky bass tone, and a beat that lands with the bodily insistence of a heart awaiting bad news. A cold guitar figure enters in clipped phrases while bell-like electronics toll far back in the mix. Gibbard’s vocal melody brushes against the severe romanticism of The Sisters of Mercy’s “Marian,” while his softened, reverb-heavy timbre evokes Neil Halstead from Slowdive if he were dragged into a goth club. With each cycle, more haze collects around the vocal until the recording seems to lose its walls. Landers becomes increasingly audible behind Gibbard, turning confession into divided speech. The bass later steps forward with the high-register gravity of Peter Hook on Joy Division’s Closer, particularly the downward pull of “Twenty Four Hours.” Its dense, overdriven attack also evokes Simon Gallup during the Cure’s Pornography-era tour, when his bass occupied the front of the mix as a blunt rhythmic force and a source of dread. Gibbard explains the song’s origin: “The song came from an idea to challenge ourselves to write something around one riff and something dirge-like. It also fit the theme of the album and the topic of repetition by literally experimenting with repetition in the musical sense. The opening line – “is your mind split in two” – is something taken from our conversations on our many long walks around London where Sophie was talking about the psychological term splitting. It seemed to fit the feel of the song and theme of the album so much so it now opens up both the album and our live shows. I consider it very much Sophie’s song because she was the source of inspiration and that’s why we have her backing vocals fairly prominent to create a dual vocal effect. I also had the after-thought to have Sophie mime the first line in the video which is actually her line anyway.” The phrase “is your mind split in two” brings the album’s psychological framework down to one troubling image: a mind unable to reconcile its opposing halves. Landers’s backing vocal gives that division a second body, allowing the song to behave like a thought hearing itself repeated from elsewhere. Its central riff follows the same principle, returning with enough force that familiarity becomes confinement. Filmed by Landers and Gibbard, with the final cut crafted by Landers, the scene begins with Landers gazing directly into the camera, silently delivering the line that sparked the song. Her high-collared white blouse, black straps, braided hair, dramatic eye makeup, and black lipstick create a striking contrast against a nearly empty black background. Gibbard appears dressed in black, with close-cropped blond hair, his face illuminated by pale blue and green lighting. Their portraits alternate between clean digital images and footage rephotographed from a monitor. Vertical scan lines stripe Landers’s face; clipped highlights bleach her features into white and violet; soft focus, projection, and offset copies divide her image across the screen. Gibbard receives similar treatment as his head drifts in and out of the surrounding black. Close-ups of fingers working a bass guitar and a solitary illuminated snare interrupt the faces, then return according to the song’s circular logic. The clip’s most pointed image is a small porcelain pig figurine dropping into the frame and shattering against a black floor. Landers later restores it through editing, only for the descent, impact, and dispersal of its fragments to happen again. The sequence becomes a compact illustration of repetition compulsion: an object returns intact so that the original damage can be recreated. Faces, gestures, instruments, and breakage recur with slight mutations, making repetition the video’s visual grammar as well as the song’s foundation. Watch the video for Repetition below: Repetition Compulsion takes its title from the Freudian concept describing “the unconscious tendency to recreate familiar emotional patterns, destructive behaviours and inherited cycles from the past.” Across eleven songs, Black Doldrums examine the ways these patterns enter relationships, memory, political life, and mental health. “The album invites listeners to confront the echoes of the past while questioning whether those patterns can ever truly be broken,” says Gibbard. The trio draws upon ’80s gothic post-punk, synth-pop, and darkwave, alongside the film music of John Carpenter and Vangelis. Analogue synthesizers, chorus-treated guitars, and driving rhythms give the record a cinematic scale while preserving the melodic directness established across the previous two albums. Repetition Compulsion arrives November 13th, 2026, on 180-gram neon-yellow vinyl limited to 350 hand-numbered copies, 180-gram ultra-clear vinyl, and CD. Pre-order the album here. Repetition Compulsion by Black Doldrums Kevin Gibbard and Sophie Landers formed Black Doldrums in London as a two-piece, combining Gibbard’s guitar and vocals with Landers’s drums and vocals. Their early work drew heavily from dark psychedelia, drone, reverb, and the physical economy of playing as a duo. The addition of bass expanded Black Doldrums into a trio around the recording of Dead Awake, giving the songs a more pronounced post-punk structure. Released through Fuzz Club in 2022, Dead Awake established their colder and more direct studio approach. Its 2024 successor, In Limerence, examined romantic fixation, loss, and the unstable interior life of a relationship. The band subsequently toured extensively across the UK and Europe, including arena dates supporting Archive and their own headlining runs. Repetition Compulsion brings the trilogy to its conclusion while extending those personal questions into inherited behaviour, politics, memory, and mental wellbeing. items.album: Analog Dance Descends Into Desire and Decay on Latest Album “Mind The Fall”
items.excerpt: When we first heard Analog Dance’s recent single Fall Apart, the song seemed built from passion and pressure: a rigid beat marking the perimeter, bright synthesizers narrowing the available space, and Jonny Castle’s baritone holding its composure while the dancefloor threatens to bend and buckle from its seductive groove. items.body: When we first heard Analog Dance’s recent single Fall Apart, the song seemed built from passion and pressure: a rigid beat marking the perimeter, bright synthesizers narrowing the available space, and Jonny Castle’s baritone holding its composure while the dancefloor threatens to bend and buckle from its seductive groove. Within Analog Dance’s second album, Mind The Fall, that steamy pressure becomes one element in a larger design. Across eleven tracks and just under forty-five minutes, the London darkwave project turns collapse, concealment, desire, and performance into sensual dark electronic pop, with guitar supplying warmth or frost at carefully chosen moments. Mind The Fall, released July 22 through Poland’s Bat-Cave Productions, follows the project’s 2024 debut, Stranger Minds. Written and recorded in isolation in a wooden cabin in Argentina, the album carries the concentration that distance can bring. Its songs feel secluded and interior, while broad drum machines, elastic bass sequences, and clean guitar lines give them considerable physical force. The production is fuller and more exact than before, though the closeness of a private recording remains central to its appeal. In a 2024 interview, Jonny described Analog Dance as an alter ego created to express emotions that words alone could not carry. He also traced the project’s name to the tactile appeal of analog equipment and the ability of synthesizers to stir feeling and movement. Mind The Fall gives that idea its clearest form yet: the machines set bodies in motion, while his voice reveals the cost of maintaining control. The titles supply their own vocabulary. Wires and screens suggest mediation; masks and shows invoke presentation; decay, rot, and falling apart name what lies beneath. Even “A Clean Version of Hell” turns damage into something polished enough for display. These phrases create a thread across the record, and the music follows suit, pairing immaculate surfaces with uneasy motion underneath. “Ghost on a Wire” opens with low, fluttering synthesizers that carry a faintly occult charge, followed by a broad drum-machine strike and a simple rising-and-falling guitar figure. Jonny’s baritone enters deep, lush, and close, drawing the ear toward the center of the mix. The melody is economical enough to lodge after one pass, while the production gives every layer room to register. As an opener, it introduces the album’s governing attraction: machine precision warmed by a voice carrying unmistakable appetite. “A Clean Version of Hell” begins in metal and glass, patiently arranging hard-edged effects and cool high-register tones before a heavy ’80s drum pattern and rounded melodic bass take command. Crystalline guitar phrases hang above the rhythm as Jonny brings deep new-wave romance to the center. The title’s contradiction—hell sanitized, pain made presentable—anticipates the record’s later concern with screens, masks, and performance, while the music could easily accompany the most intimate scene in an unmade late-night thriller. “Fall Apart” gains additional meaning from its place in the sequence. The severe elegance remains: a rigid beat draws the room, the synthesizers constrict it, and unease passes from bass to percussion to the open space around the vocal. Its supple club gait occasionally recalls Boy Harsher’s more sensual turns, though Jonny’s elongated phrasing and the clean post-punk guitar keep the song firmly within Analog Dance’s own language. Positioned between “A Clean Version of Hell” and “Behind the Screen,” the lead single becomes the album’s hinge, connecting polished catastrophe to private longing. “Behind the Screen” fades in gradually, assembling drums, bell-like chimes, and broad, glassy pads in measured layers. The mood brings to mind a romantic scene from 2011’s Drive, with city light sliding across a windshield as a high guitar line curls upward through smoke. Jonny holds his notes longer here, allowing earnest tenderness to replace some of the album’s usual reserve. The result produces a quiet rush of serotonin, spacious and enveloping, with each element entering at precisely the right moment. “Five-Star Mask” starts with rippling synthesizers that recall S U R V I V E scoring one of Stranger Things’ dreamier passages. A single DX7-like digital preset flashes past—before the full dance beat settles in. Drums and bass carry the weight as a supple synthwave melody continues below Jonny’s low, sultry vocal. Glinting guitar and a buoyant ascending-and-descending motif complete an intimate midtempo dance, made for two people moving together while the surrounding room recedes. “Intimate Decay” lowers the temperature with wavering upper-register tones and a deep electronic hum, then suspends the arrangement for a breath before a rubbery bass sequence begins. Cold jolts repeat, the drums shudder, and a brief baroque figure rises and falls before Analog Dance’s favored high-register guitar enters. Jonny sustains his phrases above the accumulating layers until the texture feels nearly physical. The title’s pairing of closeness and decomposition could stand as the album’s thesis, and the track renders that friction with particular tenderness. “Same War Within” opens on gauzy pads, pinpoint synth notes, and a heavy kick before claps and a rippling bass line steer it toward Italo disco. Guitar serves as an accent at first, leaving generous space around the low vocal. A little over a minute in, the arrangement changes its balance: a burbling figure settles below the mix, the voice drops out, and the guitar takes melodic command before the two rejoin over a cool pad. That sequence of handoffs is among the album’s smartest structural moves, creating development through control rather than grandstanding. “Scenic Crime” eases the pace with subdued synthesizers, a measured drum pattern, and a bass backbone that keeps the song moving. A modest, immediately hummable keyboard melody appears, and the guitar soon traces its outline. The feeling is wistful, suspended somewhere between pleasure and loss, as Jonny’s smooth delivery settles over low melodic undertones and small electronic flourishes drift through the margins. Its emotional ambiguity gives the track its pull; the view is lovely, though something unresolved remains just beyond the frame. “Beautiful Rot” opens with distorted, icy electronics, then answers them with a rapid drum barrage and a muscular dance bass line, making this one of the record’s fastest selections. A buoyant sequence and clear bell tones prepare the entrance of Jonny’s baritone and a clean, chiming guitar, while his quicker vocal phrasing swoops around the percussion. The song turns the album’s central contradiction into movement, placing elegance and deterioration in the same body. Its speed and melodic abundance make it a late-record peak. “The Plastic Show” rides a cycling electronic sequence that remains in place while resonant chimes, low-register strings, and a cleaner guitar line accumulate around it. Jonny initially sounds more detached than he did on “Beautiful Rot,” but his delivery gathers pressure as the song proceeds. Frustration remains contained within the measured arrangement, creating the sense of somebody trying to keep up appearances while emotion presses against the surface. As the record’s clearest invocation of artificial display, it brings the album’s concern with performance into plain view. “Selling the Show” closes the album by fading into broad pads and skittering drums, immediately establishing a cinematic new-wave atmosphere. Metallic bass enters with a melodic bounce, the pace gathers, and Jonny’s voice guides the song through several cleanly placed breaks. Familiar burbling synthesizers and a luminous guitar line return, but the final vocal passages are compressed into a distant, radio-like signal. That treatment leaves the confession mediated and receding, as though private feeling has finally been packaged for transmission. Taken together, Mind The Fall draws openly from the memory of ’80s post-punk, darkwave, synthpop, synthwave, and film music, using those reference points as a working vocabulary. Analog Dance’s identity remains distinct: a low voice with considerable tenderness, forceful electronic drums, lucid guitar, and synthesizers that can suggest glass, smoke, metal, or silk. The album is sensual, emotionally exposed, and highly danceable, with pacing that gives desire and anxiety equal weight. Where Stranger Minds established the dimensions of Jonny’s private world, Mind The Fall brings its architecture into sharper focus. Recurring textures connect the songs, the titles deepen one another, and “Fall Apart” now reads as the center of an album preoccupied with the effort required to remain intact. It is Analog Dance’s most cohesive release so far, a record whose immaculate finish cannot conceal the strain moving underneath. Mind The Fall was released July 22 through Bat-Cave Productions and is available now on all streaming platforms. The physical CD edition can be ordered directly from the label, while the label’s Bandcamp offers a digital edition. Analog Dance credits Crimeframe for recording, production, mixing, and mastering, Rusty Pilgrim for artwork, and Synth Wizrd for design. Listen to Mind the Fall below or via Spotify and order it here. items.body: Diego Romo’s Are The Lovers moves with the heavy, deliberate gait of something crawling out from beneath a nightclub after closing time, wearing somebody else’s leather jacket and carrying a grin that suggests the evening went either very well…or catastrophically wrong. The 24-year-old Chilean artist drags alternative rock, post-punk, synthwave, and gothic excess into the same dim room, then lets them eye one another suspiciously over the bassline. The opening seconds establish a pace somewhere between a stalk and a crawl, allowing each low note to land with the authority of a hostile bouncer. The sinister bass is the song’s center of gravity: thick, slow, and almost indecently physical. Around it, guitars grind without turning the track into a blunt-force exercise, while electronic textures give the production a futuristic chill. Strange sucking sounds appear between phrases, an inspired bit of studio mischief that makes the song feel as though it might latch on to your neck while you are busy admiring the chorus. Romo’s voice hangs above the arrangement in sheets of echo, cool enough to seem composed yet close enough to carry an unmistakable sense of appetite. “This song is what I imagine would happen if Queens of the Stone Age and Nine Inch Nails decided to write a song for sex in the year 2079,” he says. One suspects the year 2079 will involve worse rent, smaller apartments, and considerably less flattering latex wear. Are The Lovers shares Queens of the Stone Age’s narcotic strut and Nine Inch Nails’ industrial unease, but Romo also reaches toward Depeche Mode’s decadent electronics, Type O Negative’s funereal sensuality, and the sleek night-drive menace associated with the late Kavinsky. The Horrors hover nearby in the track’s smeared textures, while the Arctic Monkeys comparison surfaces through its slow, knowing posture. Seduction becomes more interesting when a little spice enters the room. Are The Lovers plods forward with purpose, leaving enough space for every drum hit, vocal echo, and unidentifiable mouth-like noise to register. Listen to Are The Lovers below: Are The Lovers presents Diego Romo as an artist with a firm grasp of atmosphere and a healthy suspicion of daylight. His mix of rock mythology, cyberpunk imagery, vampiric desire, and electronic menace could easily collapse into costume drama, yet the song maintains a sharp sense of control. It is sensual, strange, and slightly ridiculous in precisely the right proportions, which is often where rock music starts behaving properly again. items.body: ZEU’s Existor is an album that begins with the sort of grand private wager rock records used to make before everybody became a brand manager with a ring light: one person, one room, a stack of machines, and enough nerve to build a small city out of doubt. ZEU, pronounced “zoo,” is Matthew Zedolik of Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, and he handles the writing, playing, recording, and production himself. That arrangement can produce either magnificent obsession or twelve tracks of a man arguing with his presets. Here, obsession wins by several lengths. Zedolik describes his approach as “’80s-era Springsteen meets Billy Idol, Depeche Mode, and Sisters of Mercy.” It sounds like a barroom dare issued after somebody fed the jukebox three dollars and locked all the exits. Existor carries that collision with uncommon coherence. Drum machines march beside broad synthesizers, guitars supply muscle and abrasion, and the songs keep returning to direct pop shapes even when the lyrics are busy examining memory, age, desire, disappointment, and the cash-register logic infecting ordinary relationships. Zedolik’s background helps explain the album’s reach. Teenage metal bands taught him weight; The Ordinals gave him bass discipline; American Buffalo Ghost supplied guitar mileage; recording studies in New York sharpened his control over space and arrangement. He brings all of it into these twelve songs without turning the record into a résumé with drums. The parts serve the writing, and the writing keeps moving. Here, contemporary life has turned emotion into an exchange rate, and Existor keeps poking at the price tag until the adhesive comes off. Nobody needs another lecturer with a synthesizer; ZEU prefers hooks sturdy enough to smuggle the argument through the front door. Nostalgia, written in March 2024, marks the beginning of the album’s documented history and establishes its new-wave direction with a hook designed to lodge itself immediately in the ear. Atmospheric synthesizers spread across the arrangement while Zedolik’s thundering baritone rises above them, channeling Bowie through a repeated vocal phrase that feels closer to a public chant than an intimate confession. The song turns memory into something immense and communal, giving private recollection the scale of a crowded room singing the same words back at the stage. Sympathy‘s character falls somewhere between the grave authority of the Sisters of Mercy and the brisk rhythmic snap of the English Beat, with dark guitar and keyboard textures carried forward by an unexpectedly nimble pop current. At its center sits the album’s bluntest conclusion, “Sympathy is never free,” a line delivered less as wounded revelation than settled economic fact. The compact Reckoning strips away much of the surrounding machinery for a sparse ballad that recalls Peter Murphy’s theatrical poise and the Gun Club’s scorched romanticism. Zedolik leaves greater space around the vocal, allowing each phrase to land with the weight of an overdue admission. Together, the three songs frame Existor as a record about accounting in every sense: years spent, affection owed, compromises concealed, debts carried forward, and personal myths steadily losing value under the pressure of experience. Existor is severe, catchy, and suspicious of every emotional transaction. It leaves the listener wondering who benefits, who pays, and whether the receipt was printed before the conversation even began. Listen to the album below, and order it here. Existor by Zeu Released through Wilkes-Barre imprint Everything Evaporated, Existor is ZEU’s eighth full-length album, which means this private factory has been running for years while much of the music business was busy inventing new names for layoffs. Mike McTague’s artwork gives the project a face, as Zedolik helms the controls, building pop songs from accumulated experience and present-tense unease. The result feels built for headphones, highways, and anyone who distrusts a cheerful invoice. items.body: Welcome once again, Hellions one and all, to the Death's Door mid-year report. Pop a squat and listen to our objectively correct opinions on 2026's current output. We are the overlords, and our word is law.JK (kind of). We sure as hell listen to a lot of death metal around here, and 2026 has thus far been an interesting beast in this particular branch of the extreme music tree. While all of the albums listed here have received a significant amount of spin over the past several months, I feel much less sure of my list placements than I normally do at this point of the year. Sure, a host of these selections will end up in my top 25 come years end, but in what order lord only knows. The genre has felt more slippery than we've become accustomed to over the past few years, and I would classify that as a cause for celebration. Death metal is evolving, expanding, contracting, and bludgeoning with a weird sort of force this year and I'm all the way here for it.Below you'll find the albums Eden and I have enjoyed the most so far this year, and there are some potential classics among their ranks. As is tradition, we always love to hear what's been speaking to you at the year's mid-point. So always feel free to leave your picks in the comments of our socials. We won't judge you (too harshly). Death metal. Forever.-Jonathan AdamsTop 10 of 2026 So FarJonathan’s ListCryptic Shift - Overspace and SupertimeFans of the more esoteric, technical, and progressive sides of death metal have been eating GOOD over the past few years. Blood Incantation, Tomb Mold, Archspire, Fallujah, An Abstract Illusion, Horrendous, and Ulthar have been burning that particular candle brightly with releases that yours truly still listens to on a regular basis. Back in 2020, Cryptic Shift landed squarely in the ranks of these greats with their debut record Visitations from Enceladus. It’s an excellent collection of tracks that certainly pointed toward even more thrilling things to come, but nothing contained in that record could have prepared me for the sheer mindfuckery awaiting my unsuspecting ears in their sophomore full-length, Overspace and Supertime. Proggy, technical, thrashy, bombastic, sci-fi drenched, and slathered in god-tier riffs, it’s an opus for the ages and far and away the best death-adjacent record of 2026. If there were one word I could use to describe the journey Overspace and Supertime takes listeners on, that word would be epic. Both in length and compositional ambition, there’s little left off the table when it comes to Cryptic Shift’s songwriting approach. These are utterly gargantuan compositions that feel like worlds unto themselves in terms of sheer scope, but credit must be given to the band’s militant approach to synchronicity. Every track, every riff, every weird ass interlude feels planned and rehearsed with exacting detail, rivaling (and in several ways surpassing) Blood Incantation’s Absolute Elsewhere in terms of sheer spectacle and audacity. It’s a truly brilliant display of a band’s talent coming to full fruition. If there were a second word I would utilize to describe the best possible listening experience of this record, it would be surrender. Clocking in at nearly an hour and a half, this thing is the Titanic of technical thrash/death records. There’s so much here that skipping through tracks is almost an impossibility. Lately, records of such length have been a huge turnoff for me. Three minutes of acoustic noodling in the middle of a track does not a good album make, but Overspace and Supertime is shockingly bereft of excessive bloat. Each track here unfolds, contracts, expands, and bristles with a propulsive life that is as fun and engaging an experience I’ve ever had with an album of this runtime. The more you allow it to take you on the journey it’s created, the more enriching your experience will be. So open your third eye and let Cryptic Shift transport you. You won’t be disappointed. It’s my favorite genre release of the first half of 2026 by a country mile, and I have a hard time imagining a world where it gets supplanted in the back half of the year.  Overspace & Supertime by Cryptic Shift Immolation - DescentThere’s absolutely no reason that Descent, old school kings Immolation’s twelfth full-length studio release, should be as good as it is. Yet here I sit, writing about it as my second favorite death metal release of 2026 so far. It deserves the accolade in spades. Building upon the band’s resurgence starting with 2016’s Atonement, Descent is the meanest, tightest, and most straightforwardly punishing record of Immolation’s late career. Band mainstays Bob Vigna and Ross Dolan in particular deliver some of their most engaging and punishing performances to date, leveling cities with tracks like “The Ephemeral Curse” and “Adversary” that are replete with crushing and off-kilter guitar work and vocal nastiness. There’s an energy to Descent that feels both inevitable and undeniable, culminating in one of the band’s best overall records to date. There’s plenty here for fans old and new to enjoy, and I can’t stop listening to it. Fantastic stuff from the legends.  Descent by Immolation Mylingar - ÚtThere’s no band in the death metal space that peddles as much uncompromising nastiness as Sweden’s Mylingar. Since the release of their debut Döda vägar back in 2016, Mylingar has shared a sonic space occupied by early Altarage, Ulcerate, and Revenge in terms of pure dissonant lethality, but also sound nothing like these bands in terms of execution. Mylingar’s is a sound that’s as close to an embodiment of utter sonic hopelessness and violence as I have ever heard, and Út may be the closest they’ve come to perfecting that sound. It’s bleak, chaotic, deeply unhinged, and thoroughly nihilistic to the nth degree, and while this sound may exhaust some, it utterly transfixes me. As a soundtrack to our current cultural Armageddon, I can think of nothing more fitting and spiteful. It’s a masterclass in dissonance that I cannot recommend highly enough.  Út by Mylingar Funebrarum - Beckoning the Void of Eternal SilenceFunebrarum’s second full-length The Sleep of Morbid Dreams is, in my not-so-humble and quite obnoxious opinion, the best example of effective old school death metal revivalism that I’ve heard in the 21st Century. An utter barrage of punishing and riff-forward death metal goodness, I have always held the opinion that it would be hard to top. The band’s third full-length release doesn’t quite reach those epic heights, but doesn’t need to. It’s a doom-laden and sonically destructive affair that more than competently lives up to the reputation the band have established, and I find myself not even remotely disappointed by it. Phil Tougas is on a roll as of late, and his guitar work here is as measured, effective, and punishing as I’ve heard from the master in years. It may not eclipse its all-timer forebears, but that’s unnecessary for it to still be one of the finest slabs of death metal to be released thus far this year. A genuinely fantastic return.  Beckoning the Void of Eternal Silence by FUNEBRARUM Archspire - Too Fast to DieThere are arguments to be made about each of Archspire’s previous three releases being their apex, but to my ears Too Fast to Die is the band’s most complete release. Not quite as adventurous as Bleed the Future but every bit as hooky as Relentless Mutation, Too Fast to Die feels like the measured, airtight culmination of everything the band has set out to achieve with their music thus far. It’s memorable, fast as all hell, and as fun as anything in their catalog. Have listened to this thing several times and am not coming anywhere close to being tired of it. It’s Archspire doing what Archspire does best, and I’m all the way here for it.  Too Fast to Die by Archspire Devourment - Pious ImpietyDevourment’s triumphant return in 2019 with Obscene Majesty resulted in their most punishing, brutal, and uncompromising work since Molesting the Decapitated, and is in my mind their crowning achievement. The fact that a three track EP made this list should give you an indication of the quality of the music. Picking up where Majesty left off, Pious Impiety contains some of the band’s best material to date, presenting 11 minutes of unhinged brutality that are as complete in songwriting and execution as I’ve heard from the band. If last year’s Brodequin release tickled your fancy for all things nasty, Devourment are here to retake the throne as brutal death metal’s most talented purveyors. Short, disgusting, and brilliant. Cannot wait for another full-length release.  Pious Impiety EP by Devourment Vomitory - In Death ThroesSwedish death metal’s nastiest (and most consistent) legendary act is back with another absolute banger. 10 albums and 30 years into a storied career consisting of literally zero duds, Vomitory continue to unleash a buzzsaw hell that is a wonder to behold. In Death Throes does nothing to diminish their reputation, delivering a collection of tunes that are universally fantastic. Not the flashiest, most melodic, or overtly technical of their geographic scene peers, Vomitory have always driven firmly in the lane of straightforward, Cannibal Corpse-style death metal whose only intent is to rip your face off. Unsurprisingly, rip and tear is exactly what In Death Throes does. In similar vein to Immolation’s latest, it’s one of the best examples of an old school death metal band pounding faces by sticking to what they do best, resulting in a record utterly bereft of filler or useless noodling. Prepare to be pounded into dust.  In Death Throes by Vomitory Fossilization - Advent of WoundsBrazil’s Fossilization have been quickly on the ascent when it comes to the list of best grimy, nasty death metal bands around. Their 2023 debut Leprous Daylight was an absolute banger, and their latest release Advent of Wounds fulfills the promise of their early recordings with their most mature and adventurous record to date. Unafraid to delve into the doomier and roomier aspects of their sound, Advent is a more measured, patient, and equally punishing record that begs for repeat listens. Much more of a grower than their debut, I’m afraid this release has been less positively received. But give it time and commitment and I assure you that there’s little here to scoff at. An excellent release from a band still on the rise. Can’t wait to see where they go next.  Advent Of Wounds by Fossilization Ordh - Blind in Abyssal RealmsFrom the opening moments of “Apis Bull,” the opening salvo of Ordh’s fantastic debut Blind in Abyssal Realms, I must confess thinking to myself “…is this record this year’s Blood Incantation copy?” This was a fundamentally incorrect take. While both bands share a similar love for progressive riffs and long-form songwriting, Ordh are no one’s replicant. Blind in Abyssal Realms is a thoroughly enjoyable, songwriting-rich record that’s as confident a debut I’ve heard so far this year. Their incorporation of doomier elements helps set them apart from their peers, while their utter lack of fear in tackling mind-mending progressive sections reminiscent of Opeth’s early death metal work is admirable and deeply pleasing to the ear holes. Adore this record and am officially placing Ordh on the “bands to watch” list as their career unfolds. Great stuff.  Blind in Abyssal Realms by Ordh Stabbing - Eon of ObscenityTexas’ Stabbing are unfortunately one of the most underappreciated bands in the brutal death space. While 2023’s Extirpated Mortal Process certainly turned some heads in the scene, it’s Eon of Obscenity that to me represents their full potential. A deeply adventurous record for this particularly uncompromising space, Eon features marked improvement in songwriting and musicianship, putting on display a sonic variety that’s deeply welcome. There isn’t a dud of a track on this record, and it only grows more enjoyable with repeat listens. A lean, mean, head smashing machine of an album that is utterly unafraid of expanding into uncharted sonic territory, it’s easily one of the most ambitious and enjoyable brutal death metal records of 2026 so far.  Eon of Obscenity by Stabbing Eden’s Top Five of The Best RiffageDefect Designer - DepressantsNothing kills the vibes of an album faster than the band trying too hard. To be honest with you, it might be the binding factor of all of the music I don’t enjoy, across genres. Not to say that this is the only reason I don’t like albums, just that it’s the one that’s most common and in common between styles. The inverse is also true. Or, rather, we might say that being effortless is a necessary but not sufficient condition for an album being cool; it’s the entry ticket but not necessarily the whole show. Luckily, Defect Designer have a lot more going for them than “just” sound effortless. Depressants is impressive, tight, groovy, and wild. But it’s also effortless and I think that’s what ends up making the album so good. Even when the band are doing silly stuff, like the slowed down, creaking riff on “Daily Dose of Gloom”, barely three minutes into the album, it all feels natural. You don’t get the feeling that Defect Designer sat around in the studio saying “what kind of weird and random stuff can we add here?” but rather that this is how the music flowed when it left their brain.This makes Depressants a rarely satisfying listen, as you are swept away in a smooth storm of riffs, ideas, unexpected vocals, and inventiveness. From anyone else, the album would feel contrived and artificial. From Defect Designer, it feels keen, honed, containing just the right amount of everything to do its job without overflowing into plastic. Depressants by DEFECT DESIGNER Growth - Under the UnderI put this album right after the one above it to make sure that people understand that I don’t mind that albums cannot be ambitious for fear of being perceived as contrived. Under the Under is a massive album, perhaps the “biggest” album on this list. Growth have gone all out on it, pushing their chaotic and heavy style of progressive death metal to the brink. Whether it’s the breakneck drumming, the absolutely unhinged approach to guitar composition (which blends deathcore breakdowns, massive groove riffs, and many-noted licks) or the expressive vocals (both clean and harsh), Under the Under pulls zero punches.And yet, just like Depressants above it, it feels like it fits in seamlessly. Here it’s like a flow and more a meticulous work of welding, attention spent on every edge, seam, and intersection so that all of the intricate parts of the work work together in harmony. This is, at the end of the day, what contributes to the feeling of size - there’s so much happening but instead of each part standing alone, it all rises into a monolith of death metal. Sort of like the cover art of the name of the band would imply, a tower spiraling above you, facets blending into one edifice. Under The Under by Growth Temple of Void - The CrawlBaby, you know I can’t resist heavy metal in my death metal! The Crawl is such a tasty example of how to do that, blending flamboyant, heavy metal licks with absolutely filthy death-doom riffs and deep, aggressive vocals. From the first second of the album and all the way to its end, The Crawl is in service to one thing and one thing only - the riff. Whether that’s a pummeling, armor-clad piece of death metal steel or a flashy, emotive flash of the heavy metal blade, Temple of Void understand what makes a guitar work and how the rest of the elements on the album work with the instrument. The Crawl by Temple Of Void The Blind Philosopher - InnergazerProgressive death metal seems to be having a moment in the last few years and 2026 is no different. Innergazer might be the best example, as the album is willing to draw from further and wilder influences than progressive death metal usually does. What if instead of taking notes from technical death metal and thrash, progressive death metal would be based in death-doom? You’d get Innergazer, an album that has that “fullness” of the death-doom sound but the intricacy of a progressive metal album. It took me a few listens to understand that this is what the band was going for. I kept waiting for the death-doom riffs to fully collapse and go super heavy but instead got flamboyant solos and many-noted sweeps. It was odd but once I understood that this was the intended result, I started massively enjoying the album.Opener “Indomitable” is honestly the best example of this. The second quarter of the track is dominated by this interchange, between groovy, muscular riff and over the top, verbose solos. It all ends up coalescing back into a heavy riff supporting the return of the harsh vocals but the journey along the way immediately recalls the star-dotted cover of the album. That space theme is then briefly picked back up by a touch of synths before the track once again explodes into the heavy/intricate dynamic. This dynamic sets the pace for the rest of the album, as The Blind Philosopher continue to explore just what progressive death-doom might sound like. Innergazer by The Blind Philosopher Devoid of Thought - Devoid of ThoughtOK, you know there was going to be at least one avant-garde release on this list, even though it’s a short one, right? This is it. Devoid of Thought are unsurprisingly, if you are well versed in who makes what kind of music where, Italian. Their self titled sophomore release belies the fact as agile and unpredictable drums blend with even more unpredictable guitars to create an album that I can only describe as “a miasma”. It’s hard to overstate the degree to which Devoid of Thought is hard to pin down; it is constantly swirling, pinging between complex progressive time signatures that feel on the verge of fusion jazz and a sort of churning, deep, oppressive death-doom. There is very little thought (get it) to the orientation of the listener, of course by design, as the compositions explore the fruitful spaces between these sounds. And then there’s also ambience and even drone, spoken word, and, of course, a high flying science fiction concept backed by effect-laden vocals. In short, press play on this one to hear it for yourself and give it some time to simmer. There are a lot of flavors in this soup. Devoid Of Thought by Devoid Of Thought

items.body: Heavy Blog loves Beaten to Death. Like really, really loves Beaten to Death. And how could we not? Album after album, the Norwegian grindcore mad scientists prove that extreme music doesn’t have to be that serious. Their off-the-wall, zany, maniacal strain of grindcore always manages to deliver a nasty punch and a laugh. Today, we’re getting a first peek at their next chapter. Vntrve arrives on October 23rd via Mas-Kina Records and promises to be a rollicking adventure through abrasive riffs, off-kilter rhythms, and ear-shredding blastbeats. Along the way, we meet a cartoonish cast of characters on psychedelic adventures: K-pop demons, dying ponies, and our melancholy protagonist, the Sunburnt Satanist.Inspired by a series of unfortunate events involving drummer Chris “Anti-Christian” Bartender having to apply corpse paint on a sunburnt face, “Sunburnt Satanist” follows a “trve kvlt Norwegian satanic warrior going on holiday in southern Europe.” Out of respect for our Nordic friend’s plight, the track is almost sedate by B2D standards, relying on moody basslines to oscillate from mad enthusiasm to grim regret. Lurching, almost jazzy, excitement accompanied by howls fades into atmospheric angst and forlorn riffs, only to ricochet into frantic shouting as our crispy hero rallies. After all, the band says: “Even the evilest of Nordic Vikings need the occasional break from the call of the winter moon.”Listen to the track below and stay tuned for Vntrve, out October 23rd. Follow Beaten to Death on Bandcamp, Facebook, or Instagram. “Sunburnt Satanist” cover art created by the band's good friend and cartoonist Kristian Krohg-Sørensen.

items.body: 2026.07.30 日伊国交樹立160周年 株式会社ヤマハミュージックジャパンと、在日イタリア大使館が、日本とイタリアの文化交流発展を目的として、パートナーシップ契約を締結した。 ヤマハミュージックジャパンは、2025年に開催された大阪・関西万博のイタリアパビリオンに協賛し、ヤマハのコンサートグランドピアノを館内に設置するなど、イタリア音楽文化の普及に携わってきた。今回のパートナーシップ契約では、グランドピアノのハイグレードモデル「S6X」がイタリア大使公邸に設置され、日本とイタリア、2国間の国交樹立160周年関連行事において演奏機会を創出する。 記者発表では、マリオ・アンドレア・ヴァッターニ駐日イタリア大使が「これからイタリア大使館とヤマハミュージックジャパンは、この大使公邸で定期的に音楽イベントを共同で開催していきます。そのイベントではオペラ、クラシック音楽、ジャズ、現代音楽、そして新たな音の可能性まで幅広いテーマを扱っていきます」と述べた。 続いて、ヤマハミュージックジャパンの松岡祐二代表取締役社長は、 「音楽がイタリアと日本の未来の関係を築くために、とても重要な役割を果たすと信じています。（中略） 私は、これまで20年海外に駐在したなかでイタリアが一番長く、本当に大好きな国。駐在時、小学校に音楽教室を広げ、多くのアーティストと活動を広げるなど、イタリアの音楽文化の普及・発展に取り組みました。（中略） ヴァッターニ大使より、日伊国交樹立160周年という記念の年に、音楽を通じて日伊文化交流を一緒に盛り上げてくれないかと言われたとき、大変嬉しく、やりましょうと即答しました。日伊160周年に相応しい文化交流、本当に楽しみにしています」と期待を込めた。 記者発表では演奏が披露された。左から、ピアニストの河原義さん、テノール歌手の笛田博昭さん、大阪・関西万博でイタリアパビリオンのアンバサダーを務めたソプラノ歌手の藤井泰子さん、同万博で「CFX」のアンバサダーを務めたイタリア人ピアニストのアルベルト・ピッツォさん

items.album: 編集雑記……58──メディアの運営のケの部分（タグどうする？会議のこと）
items.tags: art sound art contemporary music improvisation
items.excerpt: この7月から、記事それぞれの性質や属性を短い言葉で説明・表現する「タグ」を試験的に増やしてみています。 記事タイトルの上にある、「#」の付いたこういうやつです 2024年に、サイトのデザインやその裏側の更新システムをリニューアルしたartscape。ですが、翌年2025年は通常の記事の更新に加え、サイト開始から30周年の特別企画が目白押しだったりと、編集部のメンバーで日々のartscapeの運営の細部について腰を据えて考える時間がなかなか取れずにいました。どのような読み手にどのような情報を届けたいか。サイトの根幹にもっとも大きく関わるこういった「編集方針」は、30周年の節目にも対話を重ねたり再考する機会がたびたびありましたが、ページの細部のアウトプットや運営実務といったハレとケの「ケ」の部分──例えば更新頻度（リニューアル後は平日は基本的に毎日更新。その前までは毎月1日号・15日号と、どさっと月に2回まとめて公開する雑誌的なスタイルを取っていました）や編成、公開する時間、あるいはミニマルなところでいうと、記事のなかのテキストの表記ルール、そして記事の「カテゴリ」や、今回追加した「タグ」
items.body: この7月から、記事それぞれの性質や属性を短い言葉で説明・表現する「タグ」を試験的に増やしてみています。 記事タイトルの上にある、「#」の付いたこういうやつです 2024年に、サイトのデザインやその裏側の更新システムをリニューアルしたartscape。ですが、翌年2025年は通常の記事の更新に加え、サイト開始から30周年の特別企画が目白押しだったりと、編集部のメンバーで日々のartscapeの運営の細部について腰を据えて考える時間がなかなか取れずにいました。どのような読み手にどのような情報を届けたいか。サイトの根幹にもっとも大きく関わるこういった「編集方針」は、30周年の節目にも対話を重ねたり再考する機会がたびたびありましたが、ページの細部のアウトプットや運営実務といったハレとケの「ケ」の部分──例えば更新頻度（リニューアル後は平日は基本的に毎日更新。その前までは毎月1日号・15日号と、どさっと月に2回まとめて公開する雑誌的なスタイルを取っていました）や編成、公開する時間、あるいはミニマルなところでいうと、記事のなかのテキストの表記ルール、そして記事の「カテゴリ」や、今回追加した「タグ」など──に、その編集方針やアティチュードを浸透させることにもちゃんとエネルギーを使いたい（ついつい後回しになってしまいがちだけど……）ということで、ごくミニマルな一歩ですが、今回の新規タグ追加です。 タグも、もともとは連載・コーナー名（「#キュレーターズノート」「#遊歩録」「#編集雑記」など）や記事中で取り扱う美術館名に限定して記事に付けていく運用に留めていました。 とはいえ、際限なく無秩序にタグが増えていってしまうのも収集がつかなくなってしまうのでは、という懸念から、今回の追加分はかなり厳選して一度様子を見ることに。レビューなどで扱うジャンル名（のうち、「#本」「#工芸」「#パフォーミングアーツ」など解釈が比較的分かれにくいもの）、あるいは記事のスタイル（「#インタビュー／座談会」）、そして編集部が特に注目していきたいテーマ（「#エデュケーション／教育普及」など）のタグがこの7月に追加されました。 ［今回追加されたタグ一覧］ ①建築／都市（arch-urban） ②パフォーミングアーツ（performing-arts） ③本（books） ④工芸（crafts） ⑤インタビュー／座談会（talks-interviews） ⑥エデュケーション／教育普及（edu-outreach） ⑦海外／国際交流（global-relations） ⑧アートマネージメント（art-management） ⑨アートプロジェクト（art-projects） これまでも、タグについて話す機運は時折高まりつつも、「それはジャンルなのかメディアなのか」論争（？）など概念的な議論も巻き起こり、暗中模索、なかなかまとまらず。しかしこのたび仕切り直して行なった話し合いでも改めて感じましたが、編集部のメンバー一人ひとりの媒体の捉え方やその微妙な違い、そしてメディアを作り上げる言葉のトレンド変遷などまで対話のなかから見えてくる、これはこれでなかなか面白い体験なのです。 複数の記事を読み歩く感覚や、記事同士の意外なつながり、タグという観点でもぜひ注目してみていただけたら。そして今後追加してほしいタグなどがもしあれば、お気軽にSNSなどで教えていただけたら嬉しいです！（g）

items.album: 杉江あこ｜エットレ・ソットサス─魔法がはじまるとき、デザインは生まれる
items.tags: art sound art contemporary music improvisation
items.excerpt: 会期：2026/06/23～2026/10/04 会場：アーティゾン美術館［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://www.artizon.museum/exhibition_sp/sottsass2026/ 20世紀イタリアデザインの巨匠といわれるエットレ・ソットサスが、デザイナー集団「メンフィス」を結成してからもう40年以上が経つ。にもかかわらず、ポストモダンと評されたメンフィスが世界に与えた影響力は未だ計り知れず、これを超える思想性の高いデザイナーや集団は、その後も現われていない。むしろ、時代は再びモダンデザインという守りへ向かっているような気がしてならないのである。そうした意味で、本展はいまの世の中に対しても強烈なメッセージを残し得るに違いない。 「エットレ・ソットサス」展示風景 ©Yuya Furukawa 本展は日本初のソットサスの大規模回顧展であるとともに、アーティゾン美術館にとっては初のデザイン展として話題を集めている。同館を運営する公益財団法人石橋財団は、近年、デザイン分野の作品収集に注力し、中でもソットサスの初期から晩年におよぶコレクションを100点以上抱えるに至った
items.body: 会期：2026/06/23～2026/10/04 会場：アーティゾン美術館［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://www.artizon.museum/exhibition_sp/sottsass2026/ 20世紀イタリアデザインの巨匠といわれるエットレ・ソットサスが、デザイナー集団「メンフィス」を結成してからもう40年以上が経つ。にもかかわらず、ポストモダンと評されたメンフィスが世界に与えた影響力は未だ計り知れず、これを超える思想性の高いデザイナーや集団は、その後も現われていない。むしろ、時代は再びモダンデザインという守りへ向かっているような気がしてならないのである。そうした意味で、本展はいまの世の中に対しても強烈なメッセージを残し得るに違いない。 「エットレ・ソットサス」展示風景 ©Yuya Furukawa 本展は日本初のソットサスの大規模回顧展であるとともに、アーティゾン美術館にとっては初のデザイン展として話題を集めている。同館を運営する公益財団法人石橋財団は、近年、デザイン分野の作品収集に注力し、中でもソットサスの初期から晩年におよぶコレクションを100点以上抱えるに至ったという。幅広い分野の美術作品を所蔵する同館が、デザイン分野に目を向けた際、最も注目したのがソットサスの作品だったという点は興味深い。言い換えれば、美術の文脈でも十分に語れる作品だったということだろう。 「エットレ・ソットサス」展示風景 ©Yuya Furukawa 「エットレ・ソットサス」展示風景 ©Yuya Furukawa ソットサスがデザイナーとして歩んできた時代は、そのまま戦後のイタリア史および世界史と重なる。戦前にトリノ工科大学で学位を取得後、第二次世界大戦従軍を経て、1950年代からプロダクトや家具のデザインに本格的に携わるようになるからだ。彼の初期代表作は、何といってもオリベッティ社の真っ赤なタイプライター「ヴァレンタイン」である。本展は回顧展ということもあり、このように初期から晩年に向かってソットサスの来歴や作品を紹介する内容となっていた。インドを旅して影響を受けた東洋美術や、病床で描いた「トーテム」シリーズのドローイング、また数々のメタファーを表現したモノクロ写真シリーズなど、メンフィス結成に至るまでの経緯が手に取るようにわかり、彼の思想や作品に対する理解が進んだ。ソットサスからすればモダンデザインを考えることは容易いが、ポストモダン──すなわち「デザインとは何か」を哲学的に問い続けることほど難しいものはなかったのだろう。もちろん、デザインの基本姿勢は人々の暮らしや社会をより良くすることだ。しかし、その概念があまりに凝り固まってはいやしないか。ソットサスが生涯をかけて挑んだ活動にこそ、我々の頭を柔軟に解きほぐすヒントが隠れているように思う。 「エットレ・ソットサス」展示風景 ©Yuya Furukawa 鑑賞日：2026/06/30（火）

items.body: 2026年8月１日から、東京・ユーロスペースほかにて、パフォーマンス・アート「身体と空間をめぐる映画祭」が開催されます。 ── いま、パフォーマンス・アートへの関心が世界的に高まっている。 パフォーマンス・アートは、伝統的な芸術観の否定と過激な実験精神に端を発した20 世紀前半の前衛芸術運動（未来派、ダダ、シュルレアリスム、構成主義、バウハウスなど）を源流とした出自と、「一回性の表現」を残す難しさから、⾧らく美術界の片隅に配されていたが、それは過去のものとなった。 現代美術の国際的祭典として最新の動向を世界に発信するヴェネチア・ビエンナーレでは、2017年と2019年の2期連続で、パフォーマンス・アート作品が金獅子賞（最高賞）を受賞。また、2017 年にはキャロリー・シュニーマンが金獅子賞（生涯功労賞）を受賞。芸術界のノーベル賞と称される高松宮殿下記念世界文化賞においても、2023 年にロバート・ウィルソン、2025 年にマリーナ・アブラモヴィッチとアンヌ・テレサ・ドゥ・ケースマイケルというパフォーマンス・アートの巨匠たちが受賞。その躍進ぶりを象徴している。… 本映画祭では、芸術表現の周縁から中心へと躍り出たパフォーマンス・アートのシーンを創造し、革新してきた先駆者たちのドキュメンタリー5作品（4プログラム）をラインナップ。その底知れぬ世界を紐解く。 （公式サイトより） ＜上映作品＞ ■Program A カニングハム（日本劇場初公開） ■Program B ブレイキング・ザ・フレーム（日本初公開） ■Program C ある日、ピナは尋ねた…〈2Kレストア版〉（日本劇場初公開） ■Program C ピンク・シュレンマー（日本初公開） ■Program D ナム・ジュン・パイク 月は最古のTV（日本初公開） ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 ＜上映劇場・公開日＞ 上映劇場・日程が変更となる場合があります。鑑賞前に必ず各劇場にご確認ください。 ■関東 東京・ユーロスペース 8/1（土）～ 横浜・横浜シネマリン 近日公開 小山・小山シネマロブレ 9/18（金）～9/24（木） ■中部 名古屋・ナゴヤキネマ・ノイ 近日公開 上田・上田映劇 9/18（金）～ ■関西 京都・出町座 近日公開 大阪・シネ・ヌーヴォ 近日公開 神戸・元町映画館 近日公開 企画・配給：トレノバ 企画協力：深川雅文、江口正登 公式サイト：https://trenova.jp/paff/
